{{Short description|Geometric graph connecting nearby points}}
[[File:Relative neighborhood graph.svg|thumb|The relative neighborhood graph of 100 random points in a unit square.]]
In [[computational geometry]], the '''relative neighborhood graph''' ('''RNG''') is an [[undirected graph]] defined on a set of points in the [[Euclidean plane]] by connecting two points <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> by an edge whenever there does not exist a third point <math>r</math> that is closer to both <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> than they are to each other. This graph was proposed by [[Godfried Toussaint]] in 1980 as a way of defining a structure from a set of points that would match human perceptions of the shape of the set.<ref name="t80">{{citation
 | last = Toussaint | first = G. T. | author-link = Godfried Toussaint
 | doi = 10.1016/0031-3203(80)90066-7
 | journal = Pattern Recognition
 | pages = 261–268
 | title = The relative neighborhood graph of a finite planar set
 | volume = 12
 | year = 1980
 | issue = 4}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Jaromczyk | first1 = J.W.
 | last2 = Toussaint | first2 = G.T.
 | doi = 10.1109/5.163414
 | issue = 9
 | journal = Proceedings of the IEEE
 | pages = 1502–1517
 | title = Relative neighborhood graphs and their relatives
 | volume = 80
 | year = 1992}}.</ref>

==Algorithms==
{{harvtxt|Supowit|1983}} showed how to construct the relative neighborhood graph of <math>n</math> points in the plane efficiently in <math>O(n\log n)</math> time.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Supowit | first = K. J.
 | doi = 10.1145/2402.322386
 | issue = 3
 | journal = [[Journal of the ACM]]
 | pages = 428–448
 | title = The relative neighborhood graph, with an application to minimum spanning trees
 | volume = 30
 | year = 1983| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> It can be computed in <math>O(n)</math> [[expected time]], for random set of points [[Uniform_distribution_(continuous)|distributed uniformly]] in the [[unit square]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Katajainen | first1 = Jyrki
 | last2 = Nevalainen | first2 = Olli
 | last3 = Teuhola | first3 = Jukka
 | doi = 10.1016/0020-0190(87)90225-0
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Information Processing Letters]]
 | pages = 77–86
 | title = A linear expected-time algorithm for computing planar relative neighbourhood graphs
 | volume = 25
 | year = 1987}}.</ref> The relative neighborhood graph can be computed in [[linear time]] from the [[Delaunay triangulation]] of the point set.<ref name="jk87">{{citation
 | last1 = Jaromczyk | first1 = J. W.
 | last2 = Kowaluk | first2 = M.
 | contribution = A note on relative neighborhood graphs
 | doi = 10.1145/41958.41983
 | location = New York, NY, USA
 | pages = 233–241
 | publisher = ACM
 | title = Proc. 3rd Symp. Computational Geometry
 | year = 1987| isbn = 0-89791-231-4
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Lingas | first = A.
 | doi = 10.1016/0925-7721(94)90018-3
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Computational Geometry (journal)|Computational Geometry]]
 | pages = 199–208
 | title = A linear-time construction of the relative neighborhood graph from the Delaunay triangulation
 | volume = 4
 | year = 1994| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>

==Generalizations==
Because it is defined only in terms of the distances between points, the relative neighborhood graph can be defined for point sets in any {{nowrap|dimension,<ref name="t80"/><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Jaromczyk | first1 = J. W.
 | last2 = Kowaluk | first2 = M.
 | doi = 10.1016/0166-218X(91)90069-9
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Discrete Applied Mathematics]]
 | pages = 181–191
 | title = Constructing the relative neighborhood graph in 3-dimensional Euclidean space
 | volume = 31
 | year = 1991| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Agarwal | first1 = Pankaj K. | author1-link = Pankaj K. Agarwal
 | last2 = Mataušek | first2 = Jiří | author2-link = Jiří Matoušek (mathematician)
 | contribution = Relative neighborhood graphs in three dimensions
 | pages = 58–65
 | title = Proc. 3rd ACM–SIAM Symp. Discrete Algorithms
 | contribution-url = http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=139404.139416
 | year = 1992}}.</ref>}} and for non-Euclidean metrics.<ref name="t80"/><ref name="jk87"/><ref>{{citation
 | last = O'Rourke | first = J. | author-link = Joseph O'Rourke (professor)
 | doi = 10.1016/0031-3203(82)90070-X
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Pattern Recognition
 | pages = 189–192
 | title = Computing the relative neighborhood graph in the <math>L_1</math> and <math>L_\infty</math> metrics
 | volume = 15
 | year = 1982}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Lee | first = D. T. | author-link = Der-Tsai Lee
 | doi = 10.1016/0031-3203(85)90023-8
 | issue = 5
 | journal = Pattern Recognition
 | pages = 327–332
 | title = Relative neighborhood graphs in the <math>L_1</math>-metric
 | volume = 18
 | year = 1985}}.</ref> Computing the relative neighborhood graph, for higher-dimensional point sets, can be done in time <math>O(n^2)</math>.

==Related graphs==
The relative neighborhood graph is an example of a [[lens (geometry)|lens]]-based [[beta skeleton]]. It is a [[Glossary of graph theory#Subgraphs|subgraph]] of the [[Delaunay triangulation]]. In turn, the [[Euclidean minimum spanning tree]] is a subgraph of it, from which it follows that it is a [[connected graph]].

The [[Urquhart graph]], the graph formed by removing the longest edge from every triangle in the Delaunay triangulation, was originally proposed as a fast method to compute the relative neighborhood graph.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Urquhart | first = R. B.
 | doi = 10.1049/el:19800386 
 | issue = 14
 | journal = Electronics Letters
 | pages = 556–557
 | title = Algorithms for computation of relative neighborhood graph
 | volume = 16
 | year = 1980}}.</ref> Although the Urquhart graph sometimes differs from the relative neighborhood graph<ref>{{citation
 | last = Toussaint | first = G. T. | author-link = Godfried Toussaint
 | doi = 10.1049/el:19800611
 | issue = 22
 | journal = Electronics Letters
 | page = 860
 | title = Comment: Algorithms for computing relative neighborhood graph
 | volume = 16
 | year = 1980}}. Reply by Urquhart, [[doi:10.1049/el:19800612|pp. 860–861]].</ref> it can be used as an approximation to the relative neighborhood graph.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Andrade
 | first1 = Diogo Vieira
 | last2 = de Figueiredo
 | first2 = Luiz Henrique
 | contribution = Good approximations for the relative neighbourhood graph
 | title = Proc. 13th Canadian Conference on Computational Geometry
 | contribution-url = https://rutcor.rutgers.edu/~dandrade/papers/ug.pdf
 | year = 2001
 | access-date = 2024-03-24
 | archive-date = 2019-03-28
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190328183825/https://rutcor.rutgers.edu/~dandrade/papers/ug.pdf
 | url-status = bot: unknown
 }}.</ref>
